name: Triptorelin
summary: A prescription hormone drug that, with continued use, shuts down testosterone and estrogen production; approved for advanced prostate cancer and for early puberty in children.
what_it_is: Triptorelin is a lab-made version of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the brain signal that tells the pituitary gland to release LH and FSH. A first dose briefly raises LH, FSH, testosterone and estradiol; with continued use the pituitary stops responding and testosterone falls to castrate levels. In the US it is sold as Trelstar (prostate cancer) and Triptodur (early puberty); in the UK it is sold as Decapeptyl, with added uses such as endometriosis. Because the first dose stimulates testosterone, anti-doping rules ban it in male athletes.

evidence.why: It is an approved drug: controlled trials in men with advanced prostate cancer and a single-arm trial in 44 children with early puberty support its labeled uses.

status_us.label: FDA-approved (Trelstar, Triptodur)
status_us.note: Trelstar (first approved in 2000) is approved for advanced prostate cancer, and Triptodur for central precocious puberty in children 2 and older. The 2026 WADA Prohibited List bans it at all times in male athletes.

benefits.claim: Lowers testosterone to castrate levels in men with advanced prostate cancer (91% to 98% of men by day 29 across three trials)
Halts early puberty in children 2 and older with central precocious puberty (LH suppressed in over 93% of 44 children)
Treats endometriosis in women, an approved use in the UK but not in the US

risks.risk: Hot flashes (in 59% to 73% of men in prostate cancer trials)
Lower sex drive, erection problems and testicular shrinkage are expected while testosterone is suppressed; trials listed them as side effects in about 2% to 10% of men
The early hormone surge can briefly worsen symptoms: tumor flare in prostate cancer (including urinary blockage or spinal cord compression) and vaginal bleeding in children
Higher risk of diabetes, heart attack, sudden cardiac death and stroke with long-term testosterone suppression; FDA describes the risk as low
Bone thinning with long-term use, which may raise fracture risk
Mood changes, depression and seizures; in children, raised pressure inside the skull (pseudotumor cerebri) has been reported

avoid_if: Pregnant or could become pregnant (it can harm a fetus)
Allergic to triptorelin or other GnRH agonist drugs
Heart disease, diabetes, a long QT interval or a history of seizures (needs a clinician's assessment first)
Osteoporosis or other risk factors for weak bones
Male athlete in drug-tested sport (banned at all times)
interactions: Drugs that prolong the QT interval, such as certain antiarrhythmics, methadone, moxifloxacin and antipsychotics
Drugs that raise prolactin (the US label advises against using them together)

before: Testosterone (men) or LH and sex-hormone levels (children)
Blood glucose or HbA1c and a lipid panel
Blood pressure and a heart rhythm check if there are QT risk factors
during: Testosterone, to confirm it stays suppressed (men with prostate cancer)
Blood glucose or HbA1c, lipids and blood pressure, periodically
In children: LH and sex-hormone levels, height periodically, and bone age
labs.why: The labels call for confirming hormone suppression and periodic checks of blood sugar and lipids; in children, growth and bone age are tracked.

studies.title: TRELSTAR (triptorelin pamoate for injectable suspension), for intramuscular use: prescribing information
studies.people: Three trials in 277, 346 and 120 men with advanced prostate cancer
studies.finding: Testosterone reached castrate levels by day 29 in 91% to 98% of men and stayed suppressed in 93% to 96% over the treatment period. Hot flashes were the most common side effect.

studies.title: Efficacy and safety of triptorelin 6-month formulation in patients with central precocious puberty
studies.people: 44 children with central precocious puberty (39 girls, 5 boys)
studies.finding: LH fell to prepubertal levels in 93% of children at month 6 and suppression held through month 12, with no unexpected drug-related side effects.

ask_your_clinician: Is triptorelin right for my situation, or is there a better-studied option for my goal?
What should I expect when I stop, and how long until my own hormones recover?
How will we watch my blood sugar, lipids, heart rhythm and bone health while I take it?

notes_for_editor: The library files triptorelin under hormone balance, presumably for off-label single-dose use by men to 'restart' natural testosterone after anabolic steroids. I found no published trial of that use; the only support is the label's description of a brief LH/testosterone surge after a first dose, so no benefit is claimed for it. The Triptodur trial was single-arm (no control group); it is graded strong only because the drug is approved for that use. Endometriosis is a UK (Decapeptyl) indication, not a US one. Risk frequencies for metabolic, bone and mood effects are not quantified in the labels, so they are marked unknown.
